The proclamation is made in a loud voice and in יְהוּדִ֑ית (oshb:Isa.36.13, tier: byte), the Judahite-language noun the verse itself carries, rather than the Aramaic the officials had just requested as narrated story content in the preceding unit; neither witness labels this proclamation 'Hebrew'. A second royal-messenger formula opens immediately at web:Isa.36.14, “The king says, ‘Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you; for he will not be able to deliver you.” (web:Isa.36.14), in Hebrew כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל יַשִּׁ֥א לָכֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֥י לֹֽא יוּכַ֖ל לְהַצִּ֥יל אֶתְכֶֽם (oshb:Isa.36.14, tier: byte), and a third opens at web:Isa.36.16, “Don’t listen to Hezekiah, for the king of Assyria says, ‘Make your peace with me, and come out to me; and each of you eat from his vine, and each one from his fig tree, and each one of you drink the waters of his own cistern;” (web:Isa.36.16), in Hebrew אַֽל תִּשְׁמְע֖וּ אֶל חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ אִתִּ֤י בְרָכָה֙ וּצְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔י וְאִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ גַּפְנוֹ֙ וְאִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵנָת֔וֹ וּשְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵי בוֹרֽוֹ (oshb:Isa.36.16, tier: byte), both still spoken under the Assyrian king's own frame rather than Yahweh's; this same verse also carries a parashah SAMEKH mark (single-witness), oshb:Isa.36.16. The unit runs to its own rhetorical climax at web:Isa.36.20, “Who are they among all the gods of these countries that have delivered their country out of my hand, that Yahweh should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?’”” (web:Isa.36.20), before the officials' silence closes the scene in the following unit.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: This short unit turns on an audience question rather than on a new speech frame: at web:Isa.36.11, “Then Eliakim, Shebna and Joah said to Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Don’t speak to us in the Jews’ language in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.”” (web:Isa.36.11), the officials ask the Rabshakeh to switch languages so the people on the wall cannot follow; the request for Aramaic is narrated STORY CONTENT here, not a label on the verse's own language, which remains Hebrew throughout the staged extract. The Rabshakeh's refusal follows at web:Isa.36.12, “But Rabshakeh said, “Has my master sent me only to your master and to you, to speak these words, and not to the men who sit on the wall, who will eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?”” (web:Isa.36.12), in Hebrew וַיֹּ֣אמֶר רַב שָׁקֵ֗ה הַאֶ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤יךָ וְאֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣נִי אֲדֹנִ֔י לְדַבֵּ֖ר אֶת הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה הֲלֹ֣א עַל הָאֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַיֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל הַ֣חוֹמָ֔ה לֶאֱכֹ֣ל אֶת חראיהם צוֹאָתָ֗ם וְלִשְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת שיניהם מֵימֵ֥י רַגְלֵיהֶ֖ם עִמָּכֶֽם (oshb:Isa.36.12, tier: byte), itself a doubled ketiv/qere verse (single-witness apparatus) and the site where the Rabshakeh's own title again surfaces as two separate tokens rather than one compound word, visible in the same pointed quote above. The same verse carries two distinct adonai-family forms rather than one form repeated: the second-person-singular-suffixed אֲדֹנֶ֤יךָ (oshb:Isa.36.12, tier: byte) and the first-person-singular-suffixed אֲדֹנִ֔י (oshb:Isa.36.12, tier: byte), distinct from each other at byte tier and at finals-normalized skeleton tier alike; only the second is a member of the book's bare hiriq-pointed adonai census, which stands at exactly three verses (MT 36:8, 36:9, 36:12). Both tokens name the human master relation rather than the divine title. This row closes with the Rabshakeh's own crude threat, before he turns to address the wider audience directly in the next unit.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: This unit opens at web:Isa.37.1, “When King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into Yahweh’s house.” (web:Isa.37.1), pointed at its own onset as וַיְהִ֗י כִּשְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ (oshb:Isa.37.1, tier: byte) — a verse-initial wayehi-plus-temporal-infinitive clause naming an explicit new grammatical subject, the king himself, in place of the delegation that closes the preceding unit. That construction, verse-initial wayehi at exact token match, stands at seven verses book-wide (sweep: 7 verses), four of them in this narrative zone, oshb:Isa.36.1, oshb:Isa.37.1, oshb:Isa.37.38 and oshb:Isa.38.4, and only oshb:Isa.36.1 and this verse pair it with both a temporal frame and an explicit new subject, the same scene-onset architecture the whole narrative block itself opens with at oshb:Isa.36.1. Hezekiah then sends his own delegation to the prophet at web:Isa.37.2, “He sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz.” (web:Isa.37.2), Hezekiah's own sending of a sackcloth-clad delegation to Isaiah. Their message names Hezekiah's own royal-messenger frame at web:Isa.37.3, “They said to him, “Hezekiah says, ‘Today is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of rejection; for the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to give birth.”” (web:Isa.37.3), in Hebrew וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלָ֗יו כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ יוֹם צָרָ֧ה וְתוֹכֵחָ֛ה וּנְאָצָ֖ה הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּ֣י בָ֤אוּ בָנִים֙ עַד מַשְׁבֵּ֔ר וְכֹ֥חַ אַ֖יִן לְלֵדָֽה (oshb:Isa.37.3, tier: byte) — that formula belongs to the king of Judah himself, not to the Assyrian king and not to Yahweh, a second frame-owner inside this same narrative zone. Isaiah's own reply opens a divine frame at web:Isa.37.6, “Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master, ‘Yahweh says, “Don’t be afraid of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.” (web:Isa.37.6), in Hebrew וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶם֙ יְשַֽׁעְיָ֔הוּ כֹּ֥ה תֹאמְר֖וּן אֶל אֲדֹנֵיכֶ֑ם כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אַל תִּירָא֙ מִפְּנֵ֤י הַדְּבָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁמַ֔עְתָּ אֲשֶׁ֧ר גִּדְּפ֛וּ נַעֲרֵ֥י מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁ֖וּר אוֹתִֽי (oshb:Isa.37.6, tier: byte) — the tier-1 object distinct from both human messenger formulas already seen. The unit closes with Yahweh's own word through Isaiah at web:Isa.37.7, “Behold, I will put a spirit in him and he will hear news, and will return to his own land. I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.”’”” (web:Isa.37.7).
